title: Joshua 13:1–7
context: Joshua 13 opens the second half of the book, which turns from conquest to the allotment of the land. Joshua is old, and God lists the territory that still remains, including the Philistine coastal plain and northern regions toward Lebanon and Hamath. God promises to drive out the inhabitants and tells Joshua to allot the land now to the nine and a half western tribes. Both traditions read this as shared ground: God’s promise is sure while its fulfillment unfolds over time. Some place names cannot be located with certainty.

verses.text: Now Joshua was old and well advanced in years. The LORD said to him, “You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to be possessed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua is old, and God tells him that much land remains to be possessed. The conquest narratives give way to the allotment of the land.

Arminian readers see God speaking honestly about unfinished work. The people still have a role in taking what God gives.
verses.reformedNotes:
God addresses Joshua’s age and the remaining task together. The work will outlast the leader.

Reformed readers see God’s purpose continuing beyond any one servant. Both traditions read this as shared ground: the promise is sure, and its fulfillment unfolds over time.

verses.text: “This is the land that still remains: all the regions of the Philistines, and all the Geshurites;
verses.arminianNotes:
The land that remains includes the Philistine regions and the Geshurites. The list begins in the southwest.

Arminian readers see a realistic accounting of what is still to be done. God does not pretend the task is finished.
verses.reformedNotes:
God names the territories precisely. The list shows that the promise extends beyond what Israel already holds.

Reformed readers see the scope of God’s gift laid out before it is fully received. Both traditions read the list constructively, as a map of promise rather than a mere record of failure.

verses.text: from the Shihor, which is before Egypt, even to the border of Ekron northward, which is counted as Canaanite; the five lords of the Philistines; the Gazites, and the Ashdodites, the Ashkelonites, the Gittites, and the Ekronites; also the Avvim,
verses.arminianNotes:
The remaining land runs from the Shihor, near Egypt, to Ekron, including the five Philistine lords of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, and the Avvim. The Shihor’s exact identification is uncertain.

Arminian readers see specific, named challenges ahead for Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
The five Philistine cities are listed by their peoples. They will remain significant in Judges and Samuel.

Reformed readers see God’s word anticipating Israel’s later history. Both traditions read this geographical detail as shared ground, holding identifications of some places with appropriate caution.

verses.text: on the south; all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, to Aphek, to the border of the Amorites;
verses.arminianNotes:
The list continues with Canaanite land, Mearah of the Sidonians, Aphek, and the Amorite border. Some of these places cannot be located with certainty.

Arminian readers see the breadth of territory God intends to give.
verses.reformedNotes:
The northern coastal regions are added. The list reaches toward Phoenicia.

Reformed readers see the promise defined by God, not by Israel’s achievements so far. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and both acknowledge that the precise locations of some names are debated.

verses.text: and the land of the Gebalites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrise, from Baal Gad under Mount Hermon to the entrance of Hamath;
verses.arminianNotes:
The land of the Gebalites, all Lebanon, and the region from Baal Gad under Mount Hermon to the entrance of Hamath are included. The Gebalites are often linked with the coastal city of Byblos.

Arminian readers see a large promise stretching far north.
verses.reformedNotes:
The northern boundary reaches toward Hamath. These limits match other descriptions of the promised land, such as Numbers 34:8.

Reformed readers see God’s generous intention for his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground, without claiming certainty about every location.

verses.text: all the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth Maim, even all the Sidonians. I will drive them out from before the children of Israel. Just allocate it to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you.
verses.arminianNotes:
God promises, “I will drive them out,” and tells Joshua to allocate the land to Israel as an inheritance. Distribution comes before full possession.

Arminian readers see a promise that calls for Israel’s faithful participation in taking the land.
verses.reformedNotes:
God himself will drive out the inhabitants. Joshua’s task is to allot the land by faith in that promise.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign commitment as the ground of Israel’s confidence. Both traditions agree that God’s promise and Israel’s obedience belong together here.

verses.text: Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua must divide the land among the nine and a half tribes west of the Jordan. The eastern tribes already have theirs.

Arminian readers see orderly fulfillment of God’s promise to every tribe.
verses.reformedNotes:
The command to divide the land marks a turn in the book. Chapters 13–21 describe the allotments.

Reformed readers see God faithfully keeping his promises to the patriarchs. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the land as God’s inheritance for his people.
